### Key Takeaways

- Agentic AI architectures are set to dominate the IT industry in not-so-distant future. Yet, this emerging software architecture is still in its infancy and requires significant investment from organizations interested in adopting it.

- The new architecture adds a significant degree of complexity atop dominant microservices and cloud-native architectures, forcing architects and engineers alike to learn new concepts, techniques, and technologies.

- Many well-established fields within predominant software architecture types require rethinking or substantial adaptation to meet the unique requirements of agentic AI systems.

- Agentic AI architecture will, for quite a while, co-exist with architectures we know today until they morph into a single unified paradigm.

- The adoption of agentic AI architectures will be greatly supported by homegrown or vendor platforms that simplify and scale the delivery of complex IT products.

Most software engineers and architects are innately familiar with microservices and cloud-native architectures and have been involved in building systems based on these architectures for many years. Microservice-based systems tend to consist of tens or hundreds, and sometimes even thousands of services, responsible for different types of data processing, be it API endpoints, data pipelines, back-office workflows, and anything in between, but they do have one thing in common - they merely process data using a logic determined either by code or based on data retrieved from data stores. This doesn’t mean that such systems are simplistic - far from it. Still, despite their complexity, they can be reasoned about deterministically, which helps define and scope functionality, implement and test changes, and operate such systems, even in the face of infrastructure- or application-level failures.

All of this is about to change. Indeed, a good share of future software systems will still be deterministic and resemble what we are used to today. Still, quite soon, swathes of IT systems being designed and delivered will be leveraging AI-based solutions to power user-facing functionality. For most, if not all, architects and engineers, this will require significant adaptation to the new reality of the IT industry.

#### Related Sponsors

The adoption of AI in software architectures is driven primarily by the new capabilities that it offers, which are particularly useful for products used by knowledge workers. Historically, IT systems focused on storing, processing, and making data available via APIs and user interfaces. At the same time, humans were responsible for a good portion of data administration, utilizing business rules, procedures, office "tribal" knowledge, and their own judgment. It’s fair to point out that some, or even much, of this intelligence was built directly into IT systems to improve productivity, particularly when scaling business operations was critical. With AI-enabled capabilities, software systems can shift from operating on raw data to knowledge, thereby elevating IT's role from merely a data management and processing function to knowledge-level support for business operations and end-user functionality.

It’s difficult to gauge to what extent AI-based solutions will dominate next-generation software systems. Still, by all signs, the impact will be so substantial that we can speak about a new type of software architecture, one where AI powers large areas of functionality, making humans using products built on top of next-generation systems much more productive. Agentic AI Architecture is a software architecture in which agentic AI systems are leveraged on a substantial scale, geared towards making optimal use of generative AI (and other) models. This type of architecture builds on microservices and cloud-native architecture and adds agentic AI capabilities.

## The Emergence of Agentic AI Systems

Agentic AI isn’t exactly new, but equally, it’s not yet well established either. Over the last couple of years, agentic AI systems have evolved from simple, single-agent solutions to chains, to graphs and multi-agent systems (MAS), where multiple agents collaborate, organized in various topologies. This area is still undergoing active development, and more elaborate use cases will inevitably emerge. It’s fair to say, though, that different collaboration strategies or topologies work best for specific use cases, so choosing a simpler solution can be advantageous in many cases.

Agents make the most of the large language models (LLMs) they interact with by providing the right context. Here again, after starting with predefined prompts, the solutions gradually shifted to a dynamic context based on output from other agents, context propagation, or data fetched from external sources via retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

As the amount of context accumulated from different sources began to cause problems with diminished reasoning, engineers developed new ways of managing context, and context engineering emerged as a separate practice. The progressive context disclosure technique can further enhance the context preparation step by allowing the agent to selectively load detailed information into the context window based on the user’s prompt.

Since LLMs have effective limits on context size, the role of context engineering is to ensure that the context used maximizes the model's likelihood of producing the desired outcome, or at least minimizes the chance of hallucinations due to vague or inadequate context. Effective context engineering requires context management to store, optimize, and reuse context elements for subsequent agent invocations.

Lately, memory systems for AI agents have also emerged, enabling further enhancements to context editing. These systems organize different types of long-term memory (episodic, semantic, procedural) for storage and querying, thus allowing agents to supplement the context with past experiences/decisions, relevant facts/definitions, rules, or learned behaviors.

Context engineering has become a foundational architectural concern for agentic AI systems. It will undoubtedly continue to evolve as the needs and expectations for building and operating AI-based products grow.

Agentic AI has developed its own specialized set of communications protocols. This process was largely driven by challenges related to the complexity of agent development, the need for standardization, and the need for improved interoperability:

- Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) - designed for multi-agent systems, allows interoperability between AI agents

- Model Context Protocol (MCP) - focuses on communication between AI agents and external services (databases, tools, etc.).

## From Agentic AI Systems To Agentic AI Architectures

For agentic AI systems to be valuable, they need to be integrated into a bigger enterprise architectures. In the enterprise setting, incorporating an agentic AI system can be done by:

- Embedding an agent into a microserive exposing an API (HTTP/GRPC)

- Using an agent as an MCP tool or with A2A protocol

- Having an agent microservice consumer messages from an asynchronous channel (queue/topic)

A large-scale enterprise-level architecture may comprise many specialized agentic AI systems. Since AI agents can use MCP to use database, services/APIs or any arbitrary data sources directly, it’s important to ensure that their interactions are constrainted within a bounded context, as defined by the domain-driven design (DDD). Limiting the reach of agentic AI systems within larger architectures reduces coupling between distant or unrelated components and data sources, allowing more cohesive areas to be maintained by engineering teams without excessive dependencies or large blast radius if changes are introduced.

## Performance and Scalability of Agentic AI Systems

The scalability of cloud-based software architectures is well understood, as architects and engineers have been building and operating them for some time. The same can’t be said for agentic AI systems, where LLM call latencies are higher, and more complex multi-agent systems can further increase processing times. The performance of agentic AI systems can’t be measured solely by standard metrics such as throughput, latency, or error rates.

Researchers at Google and MIT published a paper introducing a framework for scaling multi-agent systems . The team behind the framework tested various multi-agent coordination strategies, each with several configuration parameters, including the number of LLM calls, agents, and interactions per agent. Scientists concluded that the best coordination strategy is task-dependent: financial reasoning does better with centralized orchestration, while web navigation benefits from a decentralized strategy.

The results shared by Google and MIT demonstrate that there is no one-size-fits-all approach when it comes to agentic AI, and teams building complex solutions have to experiment and empirically establish the agent coordination strategy that is best suited to the task.

## Security Challenges of Agentic AI

Incorporating agentic AI into the distributed system architecture significantly alters the security model. Agentic AI contributes additional security threats, particularly around the agent runtime, tool servers (MCP or others), and the model provider. AI agents, for instance, can be susceptible to prompt injection, instruction confusion, or tool output poisoning, leading to unintended actions or leaking data they have access to. Additionally, using external LLM models introduces risks around data residency, retention, or usage.

Furthermore, present access-control models, honed over many decades, are ill-suited to cater to agents, which can’t really be treated as human users or backend services. Cameron Pavey, senior developer at Auth0, recently proposed a new permission model specifically targeting AI agents. He argues that regular (non-AI) backend services are generally more trusted because they are deterministic and auditable, while authentication sessions and user interfaces restrict users. Agents, on the other hand, can arbitrarily trigger multi-step workflows that involve other agents and tool calls without the user’s explicit knowledge or permission.

Pavey proposes using capability-scoped permissions and task-scoped credentials as key steps toward solving the problem of agent permissions and adopting fine-grained authorization systems for layered enforcement.

It’s worth pointing out that this is not the first time that the security landscape has experienced a marked expansion. When microservices and cloud-native architectures entered the scene, we observed a shift in this area as well, leading to a revision of the access control mechanism and protocol and the emergence of now-common technologies such as JWT and OAuth .

### Key Takeaways

- Context engineering beats prompt engineering - the system that builds context matters more than the prompt itself.

- Separate context, memory, and knowledge - each serves a different purpose and should be managed independently.

- Balance history with real-time data - great agents combine experience with live signals.

- Hallucinations are often context failures - better context leads to more reliable reasoning.

- Optimize context, don't maximize it - small, relevant context outperforms large, noisy prompts.

As the industry moves from chatbots to autonomous agents, the architectural bottleneck is shifting. The hard problem is no longer simply retrieving data. It is deciding what an agent should know, when it should know it, how long it should remember it, and what should be forgotten. As with humans, it is one thing to know and another to remember. Hence, memory and knowledge. Knowing when to use any of the existing "knows" by bringing it to memory depends on the task context . For example, if I want to cook an omelet, I don’t necessarily need to remember how to knead dough right now.

Let’s break it down.

#### Related Sponsors

Agents must reason across tools, sessions, users, and live systems, given that in an engineered system we can describe the context as a control plane. Context as a control plane is an architectural paradigm in which organizational, behavioral, and situational data (the who, what, and why) serve as the centralized governing layer for system operations, rather than being hardcoded directly into individual applications, AI models, or microservices. In our world, this will determine whether an agent acts like a reliable software system. Providing the wrong context highly increases the likelihood of the model hallucinating.

Knowledge of the system is our policies, governance, and hard truth. Knowledge acts as the system’s official textbook. It holds core business logic, strict policies, and databases. Back to our omelet example, part of the knowledge would be the need for eggs and a pan.

Memory is the critical layer that bridges historical data and real-time signals into a reasoning-ready state. What needs to be remembered for the current task? This is usually information given from knowledge, historical data, and current live events.

To summarize our three components:

- Context - the immediate, active, and temporary information the agent is utilizing at any given moment. It sits directly within the model's active context window (analogous to computer RAM).

- Memory - provides persistence. It allows the agent to retain information beyond a single interaction, enabling it to learn from past experiences and adapt to users over time.

- Knowledge - the underlying foundation of facts, concepts, and rules that the agent inherently possesses before interacting with the user. It is the domain-specific data used to train or fine-tune the system, or the reference library to which it is granted access. Highly curated data.

Our goal in agentic systems is, when given the task context, system knowledge, and memory, to turn data into the right memory state at the right moment.

Beyond that, there are limitations to this dynamic architecture paradigm; hence, we need to systematically address the economic costs of large language model (LLM) limitations and the technical, architectural roots of hallucinations. As developers and architects, learning to avoid the common "culprits" of agentic systems mismanagement is crucial. Dive in to learn how to design a sophisticated, multi-tiered architecture for the next generation of reliable agentic AI.

## Shift into Context Engine

An LLM is only as good as how we use it. While the model generates, our system determines what it sees. To avoid hallucinations, we need a trustworthy system around it. Leveraging context, knowledge, and memory. To architect the system, we will separate the model from the surrounding machinery. Going forward, for the machinery around it, we will call it a context engine. The context engine is part of the context control plane. This is the orchestrator responsible for selecting, filtering, ranking, structuring, compressing, safeguarding, and delivering information before it ever hits the LLM inference endpoint. It pulls information from knowledge, categorizes it in memory, and determines what the agent's context should be at any given millisecond. This is a meaningful shift from simple prompt engineering to systems engineering.

### From Prompts to State/Context Systems

Prompt engineering assumes the task is to craft a better instruction. Context engineering assumes the real task is to build a dynamic substrate that continuously assembles the right state for reasoning. The prompt is no longer about "What should I ask the model?" It is "What is the minimal, highest-value context the model needs in order to reason well right now?"

In a production-grade agentic architecture, we require dynamic systems that dictate what an agent "knows" at any given millisecond. Our system goal is to take what’s relevant and compile a new prompt encompassing the required information to improve the model's success likelihood.

### Context as a Compiler

To understand how the Context Engine behaves, consider the analogy of a modern software compiler. A compiler translates high-level source code into machine-executable instructions; the context engine translates vast oceans of unstructured, disconnected raw, real-time, and historical data into a structured, reasoning-ready state. It builds a deterministic state machine that allows the probabilistic agent to execute safely. It ensures that inputs are authenticated, validated against business logic, stripped of personally identifiable information (PII), and securely sandboxed before the LLM generates a plan of action.

## Thinking Through Architecture

Effective software architecture for autonomous AI agents requires reconciling several fundamentally conflicting paradigms of data management and data flow.

### Historical vs. Real-Time Memory Streams

A robust agentic architecture must gracefully balance long-term "episodic" memory with immediate "sensory" input. Meaning that to build a useful context engine, our architecture must reconcile two very different categories of state: historical memory and real-time input.

Historical memory is the long-lived layer. It includes prior interactions, past decisions, user preferences, domain rules, internal documentation, and accumulated observations. This is what gives an agent continuity. It allows the system to behave as though it has experience.

Real-time input is the short-lived layer. It includes the current task, the latest events, live telemetry, fresh tool outputs, and environmental changes. This is what keeps the agent grounded in the present.

While vector databases excel at retrieving historical, semantic facts, agentic workflows frequently pivot on sub-second, real-time context. For example, if an AI DevOps agent is triaging a server outage, retrieving an architectural runbook from a vector store (episodic memory) is only half the battle. The agent also needs the live error log stream from the last five seconds (sensory memory). The architecture must fuse these batch and streaming sources asynchronously, ensuring the agent acts on a unified, up-to-date reality.

This architecture must have balance. If it over-indexes on history/episodic memory, the agent becomes stale. It will keep replaying yesterday’s assumptions into today’s reality. If it over-indexes on real-time data, the agent becomes reactive and forgetful. It may respond to the latest signal but fail to incorporate the broader context that gives that signal meaning.

Luckily for us, this tension is not new. Distributed systems have always had to reconcile durable state with transient events. Agent systems inherit the same problem, but with an additional challenge: the reasoning layer is probabilistic, expensive, and bounded by a limited context window. This adds an important layer of constraint optimization to the context architecture design - deciding which information to keep, which can be compressed, which must be revalidated, and which should be excluded entirely. The goal is not just freshness or completeness. The goal is usefulness under constraint.

Figure 1: Historical Data vs Real-Time Memory Streams (Source: created by the author with Gemini)

### Knowledge vs. Raw Data ( SELECT * vs. Cumulative Insight)

One of the most common architectural mistakes in AI systems is treating retrieval as if it were enough, ie, operating under the semantic equivalent of a SQL SELECT * , assuming more information must be better. Architectures that attempt to consistently retrieve large volumes of data will inevitably fail at scale. We can think of retrieval as how we get data into the system, yet it does not guarantee that the data is useful, timely, coherent, or appropriately ranked for the decision at hand. This is what standard RAG pipelines are all about. They are often built to retrieve raw, fragmented, and overlapping data chunks. In actuality, using this approach would most likely result in the system dumping 10 unedited wiki pages into a prompt, making the LLM waste compute cycles trying to sort the noise from the signal - yet failing due to relevant signals buried under less important and more noisy ones. Hence, the right information and shape of the data, which we refer to as knowledge , matter more than raw data.

True Knowledge Curation focuses on cumulative insight . Instead of injecting raw data, the architecture employs background workers/ML pipelines that distill, aggregate, and rank retrieved data by relevance, using the up-to-date system state. To achieve that, we need to build dedicated pipelines that transform raw data into structured knowledge graphs or condensed summaries. For example, taking a large database and creating a pipeline that summarizes a million data entries into one entry every 12 hours. This way, we ensure the model receives a small, synthesized body of knowledge (1 entry point in the database) rather than a chaotic stream of consciousness (the whole database, sometimes).

### Custom Context: The End of "One-Size-Fits-All"

Foundational models like GPT-4 and Claude, as well as vector databases like Pinecone and Milvus, have become an accessible commodity. Everyone can access them today through their services. Yet, this is not the same for context; the architectural principles for working with context are highly domain-specific. Every company should design its own context based on the business domain and the product it serves. For example, a fintech firm might choose to curate context for an autonomous fraud-analysis agent by prioritizing transaction timestamps, geolocation anomalies, and strict compliance rules. This will look entirely different for a legal tech firm. A legal tech firm might choose to curate context based on state law for use with an agent that generates contracts. We are learning that the context itself cannot be generic; it must reflect the unique domain logic, security boundaries, and vocabulary of the specific product.

# Identity as an Architectural Concern: Enterprise IAM Beyond Authentication

by

- Vaishnavi Khosla

reviewed by

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

### Key Takeaways

- Decide how identity will shape your data model during the initial design. A security review at the end can catch a missing check or a bad scope, but it can't restructure a schema that was never built to explain who had access and when.

- Once your access questions are about ownership and validity, a graph fits better than a role table. In our role tables, "who owns this account" required a chain of joins. In Neo4j, it's one traversal.

- About eighty thousand people own our service accounts. Keeping those owners engaged through job changes and departures is most of the governance work, because an account whose owner has moved on is a credential nobody is watching.

- When revocation travels over an event stream, it's eventually consistent. Know your worst-case staleness, cap it with a maximum cache age, and tell your security team what it is.

- Merging attestation, rotation, and vaulting into one workflow cut time-to-revoke from about three days to under one.

## After the Login

For a single application, identity is mostly a vendor decision. You pick an identity provider, wire up SSO, validate tokens at the edge, and move on with the features. For one application and one team, that's the right call. It stops being enough as the organization grows. Login keeps working fine. Everything after that gets difficult: who approved a given access and whether it should still exist when an auditor asks about it months later.

This article draws on building and operating an identity and access management platform in regulated financial services, where a wrong entitlement becomes an audit finding. My argument is that at enterprise scale, identity has to be treated as part of the architecture. Teams that add it late tend to find it conflicts with decisions they've already locked in. I'll assume you have experience shipping OAuth 2.0 or SSO. What follows covers the design problems that appear once many services, and many owners, are involved.

## Identity as an Architectural Concern

Identity belongs in architecture discussions because it constrains decisions that look unrelated. The data model is where this shows up first. Once you have to explain and audit access, "who can touch this resource" needs to be a relationship you can query with history, because auditors ask what was true six months ago as well as what is true today. Service boundaries and event flows raise their own problems; each gets its own section below.

#### Related Sponsors

Regulation adds another constraint. Here's a useful test: Could you answer "Who had access to this system on 14 March?" from your data model alone, without grepping logs across several tools? If not, an audit wasn't part of the design.

A security review can catch a missing check or a misconfigured scope, but it can't retrofit a schema that was never built to answer that question. The cheapest way to pass that test is to record every grant, revocation, and attestation as an event with a timestamp and an actor from the start. Then the auditor's question is one query against the event log.

## Where Flat RBAC Breaks Down

The Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) model is used by default and is usually sufficient. It strains when your questions shift from "Does this user have this role?" to how things relate to each other. Our entities are people, the service accounts they own, and the accesses those accounts hold. The questions we kept asking were: "Who owns this account?", "Is this access still valid?", and "What does this person control?"

All three are relationship questions. Ownership is a relationship. An access has a validity window and an attestation history attached to it. A person who leaves or changes roles pulls a set of owned accounts along behind them. In a role table, you rebuild each of those links with joins every time you ask. In a graph, each link is an edge and the query walks them.

That's why our backend models these relationships in Neo4j, queried through GraphQL. GraphQL fits because a query's nesting mirrors the traversal: this account, then its owner, and then its access. A caller asks for exactly the slice of the graph it needs, from an account down to its valid accesses. Nobody handwrites traversal logic or over-fetches a large object and filters it in memory. Figure 1 shows the shape of the underlying model.

Figure 1. Ownership-and-access graph modeled in Neo4j, showing how flat RBAC breaks down when access needs expiration and nuance. (Image source: created by the author.)

Before the query, here is the model it runs against. There are three kinds of nodes: Person , ServiceAccount , and Resource . There are two associations between them. First, a person OWNS a service account, while second, a service account HAS_ACCESS to a resource. The association, HAS_ACCESS , possesses some properties such as expiration , the date for when the access will be no longer valid, and lastAttested , which displays the last date when the access was attested by the owner. Validity is an attribute of the edge rather than of any node since it refers to the particular combination of the account and resource nodes.

This query, as shown below, poses a question we frequently ask ourselves: Who is the owner of this account and which of its accesses are currently valid? Looking through the query from the top, the first MATCH gets the account based on its ID and follows the OWNS relationship until it reaches the owner. The next OPTIONAL MATCH follows the HAS_ACCESS relationship towards each of the resources, and the WHERE clause appended to it filters out any access where the expiry date has expired. Because it is an OPTIONAL MATCH , an account having no accesses left will yield its owner anyway. Finally, the RETURN clause yields the owner’s name along with all the accesses left with their resources, expiry dates, and last attested date in a single array.

Neo4J Cypher Query // Who owns this account, and which of its accesses are still valid today? MATCH (p:Person)-[:OWNS]->(a:ServiceAccount {id: $accountId}) OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[g:HAS_ACCESS]->(r:Resource) WHERE g.expires >= date() RETURN p.name AS owner, collect({ resource: r.name, expires: g.expires, lastAttested: g.lastAttested }) AS validAccesses

Written as SQL against role tables, the same question needs every link lined up by hand:

-- Who owns this account, and which accesses are still valid today? SELECT owner.name, res.name, g.expires, g.last_attested FROM service_account acct JOIN account_owner ao ON ao.account_id = acct.id JOIN person owner ON owner.id = ao.person_id LEFT JOIN account_grant g ON g.account_id = acct.id AND g.expires >= CURRENT_DATE LEFT JOIN resource res ON res.id = g.resource_id WHERE acct.id = :accountId;

Even here, it's easy to get it wrong. Put the expiry check in the WHERE clause instead of the join, and accounts with no valid grants vanish from the result, owner and all. The query works, but it still leaves three problems out of view. Ownership is a single join in this example, but ownership can be delegated, and once it can, that join becomes a walk up a chain of unknown length. In the graph, the same chain is a variable-length path in one pattern. The expiry check also has to be repeated in every query that touches grants. Any query that leaves it out returns access that should have been removed. In the graph, the check sits inside the traversal, so a consumer can't skip it by accident. Finally, when a person leaves, the accounts they own aren't in front of you, and you have to go looking for them. In the graph they're one hop away, because "owns" is an edge. Both queries are simplified from what we run in production.

But Neo4j has inherent costs. It's one more datastore to operate, and traversal performance depends heavily on how you model things. A badly shaped graph can be slower than the join it replaced. It was still worth it for us, because ownership and validity are things we traverse constantly. The flat version pushes the hard part onto whoever writes the next query.

## Service Accounts: Eighty Thousand Owners, Three Tools

Comparing everything in the platform, the service accounts took the most governance work. Every service account is owned by a real person: Roughly eighty thousand people review, rotate, and vault the accounts they own. An account’s safety depends mostly on that owner: whether they're still engaged and whether they've changed teams or left the company. An account whose owner has moved on is exactly the stale, over-privileged credential that nobody notices until it's misused.

Before the rebuild, the three things an owner had to do (attestation, rotation, and vaulting) lived in three separate tools. An owner had to remember which tool did what. That's a small annoyance for someone who does it daily. For someone who does it twice a year, or who inherited an account when a colleague left, it's a real failure mode.

The rebuild put all three owner requirements into a single workflow, so an owner sees one screen with what they own and what's due. Getting there took more than wiring screens together. Each tool had been built with its own assumptions about schedules and ownership, and once they shared a workflow, those assumptions had to be reconciled. Figure 2 shows the revocation workflow before and after the consolidation: Three separate tools, with revocation taking about three days, became one unified workflow that revokes in under a day.

Figure 2. Revocation workflow before and after tool consolidation. (Image source: created by author.)

## Integrating a Vault We Didn't Own

In enterprise identity work, the risky integrations are usually the ones where your system depends on a system you don't govern. For us, that was vaulting. We already handled attestation and rotation well before the rebuild. We had written that code ourselves, so we knew how it failed. Vaulting ran in a separate tool, owned by another team, on infrastructure we couldn't change. Folding it into our workflow meant a critical control now depended on their release schedule and their outages.

The hard part was deciding what our workflow should believe when their API didn't answer, or answered slowly, or answered after our call had already timed out. Those are not edge cases when you're doing this for tens of thousands of owners. They happen every day, somewhere. So we made the integration "fail closed". If the vault was unreachable, the workflow didn't report the step as complete, and an owner was never told a credential was vaulted when it wasn't. That sounds obvious on paper. In practice it meant our side couldn't treat "we sent the request" as success. We had to confirm the vault's own state, reconcile it against ours, and treat any gap between the two as something our side resolves.

## Propagating Identity Across Service Boundaries

If every service makes its own access decisions, authorization logic ends up scattered across dozens of codebases, where nobody can audit it. When a rule changes, you hunt for it through every service that has implemented its own version, and you can miss one. What works is letting identity context travel across boundaries while the decision stays in a dedicated policy decision point. Identity propagates through scoped claims using OAuth 2.0 token exchange, so a service acting for a caller gets a narrowed token instead of reusing a broad one.

Anthropic has published how the Claude Code team runs code review now that Claude writes about 90% of Claude Code itself. The claim drawing the most scrutiny is not the percentage but what the team says it no longer needs.

The post, by Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt and Qing Wang, is the companion to Anthropic’s account of replacing git with an in-house system after its monorepo went from roughly 2,500 merged changes a day in May to more than 30,000 in September. Review was the next thing to break. The target is that most pull requests "merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents."

On comprehension, the team is explicit:

> Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don’t think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.

That passage dominated the Hacker News discussion , where commenter jonahx set out what it trades away:

> There is no longer anyone to turn to if this system breaks by, eg, having a critical bug that no one can figure out. No causal model in anyone’s head that can be appealed to, to slowly and methodically debug. The new trust model is: We trust Claude to always understand the system enough to debug anything or make any reasonable change we could want.

He also noted that many large legacy systems already work this way.

One documented case tests the explainer claim on Anthropic’s own repository. In August, Claude Code collaborator Boris Cherny answered a long-running complaint about issue auto-closure in a comment carrying the "Generated with Claude Code" footer. It said issues are closed when they have "had no activity for a while and are missing information needed to reproduce," and that "nothing is triaged solely by counting."

The repository’s issue-lifecycle.ts sets fourteen days to stale and fourteen more to closure, exempting only issues with ten or more upvotes. Developer marcindulak counted more than 6,000 issues labelled as carrying reproduction steps that were closed anyway as "inactive for too long." The remedy the comment offered, commenting to have an issue reopened, is blocked by a workflow that locks closed issues after seven days. That meta-issue is now locked.

> The answer that started this issue, and misdiagnosed how issues in this repo are managed, was generated by a world-class model.

The failures the post documents are specific. The first appears only when both sides are machines:

> Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review.

"One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it," the team writes. Running more rounds by default made things worse, so they capped them. On r/ClaudeCode , commenter ChemicalExcellent463 reported reaching the same control independently, stopping after two failed fixes because repeated failure means the agent’s picture of the code is wrong rather than the line it keeps editing.

The second failure is what those rounds were finding:

> When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer’s first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round.

What gates a merge is a risk tier picked by a classifier, where "the change sets the tier, not the author." Low risk covers docs, copy, and additive changes behind a flag, and clears with no human approval. Medium risk, including caching, the auto-updater, and system prompts, needs one person. Two rules hold the line: "an agent’s approval never counts as a person’s," and the person who prompted a change "counts as one of the required reviewers."

That boundary drew a question the post does not answer. Reddit commenter Oximy-Naman asked whether low risk covers agent instruction changes shipped as documentation, since those "could change what an agent does without touching application code," and got no reply. The post assigns no tier to CLAUDE.md , the file its own reviewer loads on every review. On compliance, Hacker News commenter gaal_dornick reported that their own SOC 2 reviewer required every change to be seen by a second human before production; the post does not discuss audit requirements.

One control is missing, and the team says so:

> We don’t yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.

Not everyone reads this as reckless. Commenter cheema33 argued that large organizations have never had anyone holding a complete model, making this an upgrade on the status quo, and commenter markbao reported spending a few thousand dollars a month on AI review against human review that consumes up to a third of an engineer’s time.

Parts of the system ship publicly. Code Review for Claude Code is generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and the security review runs as an open-source GitHub Action whose README states that it "is not hardened against prompt injection attacks and should only be used to review trusted PRs."

# Cloudflare’s Post-Quantum GeoKey Manager Enters Closed Beta without Attribute-Based Encryption

Oct 31, 2026 3 min read

by

- Steef-Jan Wiggers

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

Cloudflare has moved a post-quantum rebuild of GeoKey Manager into closed beta, protecting geographically fenced decryption keys with a hybrid of ML-KEM-768 and X25519 and replacing the attribute-based encryption the service has relied on since 2022. The beta opened on October 23 to existing Data Localization Suite customers, with general availability planned for the first quarter of 2027.

Chetan Agrawal, Arka Nayan and Erik Engstrom describe the redesign as addressing two requirements at once: data sovereignty rules that confine plaintext processing to a region, and harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks in which traffic captured today is decrypted once a quantum computer exists. GeoKey Manager first shipped in 2017 for TLS keys and moved to ciphertext-policy attribute-based encryption in 2022. Cloudflare gives two reasons for dropping that scheme: no production-ready post-quantum variant exists, and customers don't need the large number of regions it was built to express.

In its place, key protection uses HPKE, the hybrid public-key encryption construction defined in RFC 9180 , with a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) combining ML-KEM-768 and X25519, HKDF-SHA-256 and AES-256-GCM. Two kinds of keys replace the policy expressions. Regional root keys are 256-bit symmetric secrets held one per region. Application-specific key pairs are derived from a root for a single service, such as Tunnel or Gateway, and a single epoch, Cloudflare's term for a key generation that rotation advances. The key-management service derives the application key pair and wraps customer private keys under its public component.

(Source: Cloudflare blog )

The two kinds of keys travel different paths: Quicksilver, Cloudflare's globally replicated key-value store, carries wrapped keys and metadata everywhere, while regional root keys move a separate path through the provisioning service, which stores them in Vault. Before an edge server receives a root key, it must clear three checks: TPM hardware identity verification, a lookup in Zinc, Cloudflare's server inventory, that maps the identity to a data center and location, and a decision by the provisioning service about which roots that server may hold.

Authorized servers then load regional root keys into the kernel keyring rather than onto disk. Because that memory is volatile, "a machine restart removes the keys," and the server has to authenticate again. Regional membership refreshes several times a day as the network changes, separately from key rotation and without customer action.

Dabeer Shaikh , a senior solutions engineer at HashiCorp, asked under Cloudflare's announcement how a geo-fenced key can be rotated without downtime, and the post answers that question through its epoch model. A soft rotation creates a new epoch while a limited number of previous epochs stay usable, so customers keep uptime during the transition; a hard rotation rewraps affected keys under a replacement epoch and removes access to the previous one.

Mark Tehrani , founder of CyberSeQ and a professor of cybersecurity, posted five questions on the same thread. Four concern the blast radius of a compromised regional root key, whether a compromised Zinc inventory or provisioning service could hand regional keys to an out-of-region server, what protects keys exposed before a rotation, and whether a compromised control plane could alter regional membership. The fifth goes to the design's central tradeoff:

> If regional key provisioning, synchronization, or rotation fails, could the fail-closed design cause a region-wide service outage?

Cloudflare's post is explicit about that behavior. Any failed check on service context, region, or epoch rejects the request, and at the edge a missing or malformed key means the service does not start. The authors call failing closed "a very intentional design choice." The trust boundary covers the key-management, provisioning, and authorized edge key services; Quicksilver sits outside it because it only ever holds wrapped keys and metadata.

The rebuild extends a pattern in Cloudflare's post-quantum work. As previously reported on InfoQ , Cloudflare adopted hybrid ML-KEM for its IPsec service in March, when over 60% of human-generated TLS traffic on its network already used it, and the company has since set out plans for a quantum-safe certificate authority . Most regions will be covered at launch, with product-specific caveats. What the beta will show is whether the design's answer to a failed check, refusing to serve, is one customers accept at regional scale.

# Kubernetes Confidential Containers Get Fortanix Attestation and Key Management

Oct 31, 2026 2 min read

by

- Mark Silvester

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

Fortanix has announced support for Confidential Containers in its Confidential AI platform. The integration connects Kubernetes workload attestation to encryption-key release, so workloads that meet security policy can decrypt models and sensitive data inside hardware-based trusted execution environments (TEEs).

Confidential Containers (CoCo), a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project, runs Kubernetes pods inside confidential virtual machines backed by hardware-based trusted execution environments (TEEs). Unlike ordinary containers, whose isolation depends largely on the host operating system, confidential VMs use hardware protections to encrypt memory and restrict access to the workload while it runs. This helps protect data in use, not just data at rest or in transit, and can let teams run sensitive workloads on shared infrastructure. Those protections still depend on trusting the guest software and configuring attestation and key release correctly.

Fortanix's technical overview describes plugins connecting CoCo workloads to two services: Confidential Computing Manager (CCM), which verifies the environment, and Data Security Manager (DSM), which releases keys only to environments CCM has verified. The company says CCM can attest the processor and graphics processing unit (GPU) together, a check that depends on configuration.

CoCo moves image pulling and unpacking into the confidential guest. Its Attestation Agent collects hardware evidence, and its Confidential Data Hub obtains secrets after verification. In Fortanix's described workflow, keys stay in DSM if attestation fails, so the workload cannot decrypt protected models or data.

Fortanix chief product officer Anuj Jaiswal said in the announcement: "With attestation and key management in one platform, teams can adopt standard CoCo without building the trust layer themselves." Fortanix says CCM and DSM run clustered, with 24x7 support, as a hosted service, on-premises or air-gapped.

Fortanix's Intel TDX deployment guide offers two GPU settings: Required makes CCM validate GPU evidence through NVIDIA's attestation service; Ignored checks only that evidence is present and disregards the result. The guide also notes that the Fortanix CoCo Helm chart does not configure host firmware or kernel settings, which must be completed beforehand.

Attestation and conditional secret delivery already exist in CoCo's open-source Trustee components. Trustee separates evidence appraisal from resource authorisation. Its attestation service compares platform claims with reference values, then its Key Broker Service applies a user-defined policy before releasing secrets from local storage, a plugin or an external key store. A successful attestation still requires that policy to authorise the request. Trustee also accepts GPU evidence bound to the processor's attestation report.

Microsoft's Azure Secure Key Release offers a managed alternative in Key Vault Premium and Managed HSM, integrated with Azure Attestation. It releases exportable keys, not secrets or certificates.

The pod's guest kernel and helper processes sit inside the trust boundary, so teams must trust them too. CoCo's trust model explains that hardware measurements usually cover the guest environment, with container verification forming a separate stage. It also warns that an enclave application can still expose a dangerous external interface and excludes denial-of-service protection and hardware side channels. Attestation does not establish that an AI application handles data safely.

Fortanix says CoCo support is available now, and its deployment guide documents installing the Fortanix CoCo Helm chart. The announcement also says Fortanix is developing open-source plugins for CoCo, without naming repositories or versions. CCM's 17 September release notes added CoCo application registration for AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization-Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP) and Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX).

# Entire's Git Forge Rethinks Git Collaboration for Coding Agents

Nov 08, 2026 3 min read

by

- Sergio De Simone

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

Entire is a Git forge designed specifically for collaboration between human developers and AI coding agents . Its premise is that traditional software development infrastructure, particularly the pull request (PR) model, is not well suited to an environment where AI agents generate, review, and iterate on code at high speed.

As Thomas Dohmke, former GitHub CEO and currently CEO of Entire, explains, GitHub and GitLab transformed human-to-human collaboration by centering it around asynchronous code reviews and version control. A multi-agent forge, by contrast, centers around the asynchronous orchestration, versioning, and auditing of AI agents working alongside humans .

Built on top of a fully distributed architecture that enables pushes up to 89 times faster than GitHub, Entire's core component is trails , which addresses the challenges AI coding agents pose to the traditional PR-based development model:

> The pull request [timeline] has become an audit log that only the agent reads. It does not provide the information for the developer to decide whether they can merge with confidence.

Trails bring the most relevant information to the top of the page in the form of eval scores that are updated on every push. These scores help developers assess whether a PR has reached a stable state or requires another iteration of agent-driven coding and review:

> Only when the confidence is high, risk is low, and all findings are cleared, the merge should happen.

A trail can be initiated from a bug report, a feature request, or manually, and can span multiple repositories. Whenever new code is pushed, a review agent running in a cloud sandbox evaluates the changes and returns a score and a rationale based on code quality, security, slop , and whether human code review is required. For example, if the slop score is orange, developers can ask their coding agent to improve the code and push a new change, thus triggering a new iteration.

> The last 5 runs and the current run are shown for each eval. We believe this is crucial as one-shot loops are often missing a critical issue. Repeating the loops and stabilizing the scores is crucial for the success of agentic coding.

Evaluation agents can be configured through Entire's interface or repository-level JSON configuration.

Review agents can suggest fixes or improvements, which remain visible in the trail while it is open. All review findings must be either resolved or closed before a merge is allowed. Developers can also configure repository-level Gates to define the conditions required for approval.

Another foundational concept introduced by Entire is continuous memory , which preserves all accumulated knowledge in the repository so that agents can reuse it across sessions rather than starting from scratch. Continuous memory is implemented by two open-source tools, entire-graph , which builds a precomputed map of the Git repository including ranked code searches, definition and callers, types and routes, and more; and entire-brain , which creates a persistent memory layer by combining the codebase map with previous agent sessions and information recorded in Git history.

> This allows agents to always have the right context at the right time, aka the "why" behind the "what changed."

As a final note on Entire, it also supports integrations with CI platforms like Buildkite and Depot.

Commenting on the announcement on Hacker News, user conartist6 expressed the view that engineers have delegated writing code to agents because of programming languages and tools that leave much to be desired. Haimantika, currently at Entire, points out that the problem has never been languages or tools, rather

> it' s that the reasoning gets thrown away between the person and the artifact. Commit messages were always bad, docs always rotted, “why is this here” was always answered by whoever remembered. Agents just made that acute, because now there's no one who remembers. That's the bit we're trying to fix. If a better language fixes it too, honestly I'd take that.

Entire is only one of several new players in the source code management arena, which also include Zed DeltaDB , Anthropic Scion , East River Source Control , Cursor Origin , Radicle , and others.

# GitHub Makes Agentic Workflows Generally Available with Isolation and Budget Controls

Nov 11, 2026 2 min read

by

- Mark Silvester

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

GitHub has made GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available. The open-source project runs coding agents inside GitHub Actions for repository tasks such as issue triage and continuous integration (CI) failure analysis. Agents start with read-only permissions, and any changes they propose are applied by separate jobs that hold their own write tokens.

That separation has limits. The project's FAQ says the protections do not automatically extend to direct write permissions or to custom jobs a workflow author adds, so the safety of a workflow depends on how it is configured. Authors can also add a GitHub Environment protection rule to require a reviewer before a write job runs.

Developers describe the work in natural-language Markdown, with YAML frontmatter for configuration. The project compiles that definition into a standard Actions workflow, which reuses existing runner groups and policy constraints, and teams can use Copilot or bring another coding agent. According to the general availability announcement , agents run in a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall, and a threat-detection job scans proposed changes before they are applied. The project entered public preview in June 2026.

Since the preview, GitHub has added support for Actions Runner Controller (ARC), its Kubernetes operator for self-hosted runners, with Docker-in-Docker (DinD). DinD runs a Docker daemon inside the runner pod so the agent can start its sandbox containers. The project's guide notes that ARC runs the DinD sidecar as a privileged container by default, a privileged component sitting alongside an agent designed around least privilege.

Spending is capped by default. GitHub's documentation prices AI Credits (AIC) at $0.01 each and sets a cap of 1,000 AIC ($10) per run. The project's enterprise controls reference adds defaults of 5,000 AIC a day, 400 AIC per threat-detection run and a 20-minute timeout on the agent step, all of which organisations can override. The gh aw forecast command, no longer experimental, estimates monthly AI credit spending, including threat detection.

In the announcement, Ben Alton, senior manager in Accenture's Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team, said: "One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone." The announcement does not explain how that figure was measured.

Engineers testing the project have taken a more cautious line. In a walkthrough of an issue-triage workflow , Sascha Mirow-Stanitzok, team lead for middleware at freenet, judged the default budget far too generous for triage and capped his runs at 100 AIC, 15 turns and 10 minutes. He also wrote that telling the agent to ignore instructions in issue text does not protect a workflow by itself, and said he would not use the same pattern for workflows that change code or open pull requests.

GitLab takes a different route with its Duo Agent Platform flows , which run on runners under a composite identity that pairs a service account performing the actions with the human user who started the request. Its triggers , such as a mention or an assignment, must come from a human user, so one flow cannot start another. That rule stops agents from chaining work across flows without a person starting it.

GitHub's FAQ says conventional Actions remain the right choice for reproducible builds and tests, with agent workflows suited to tasks that need interpretation or generation. The project is available on GitHub Free, Team and Enterprise on github.com , and the default Copilot CLI engine requires a Copilot licence.

# Google Open Sources Ambient Quality Agent (AQuA) to Diagnose Production AI Agent Failures

Nov 13, 2026 2 min read

by

- Leela Kumili

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

Google has open-sourced AQuA (Ambient Quality Agent), a reference implementation that analyzes production AI agent sessions, verifies recurring failure patterns, and investigates root causes against deployed source revisions. The tool targets silent quality regressions that conventional infrastructure monitoring can miss, such as agents ignoring user preferences or skipping required tool calls while returning successful responses.

AQuA runs alongside an agent in Google Cloud, outside its request path, reading telemetry from Cloud Trace, Cloud Logging, or BigQuery. It samples up to 1,000 recent sessions per run and processes them through five stages: sampling, reviewing, clustering findings, verifying candidate clusters, and tracking issues. Developers can configure domain-specific quality criteria through a goal.md file and add deterministic custom metrics. AQuA can run on a schedule, after a deployment, or on demand.

For root cause analysis, AQuA compares failing sessions with an immutable source snapshot captured at deployment. Its diagnosis agent identifies relevant code or instructions, cites file and line ranges, and proposes changes when the cause lies in the repository. It can also attribute failures to external dependencies, tool handoffs, or retrieved data. AQuA does not apply fixes or open pull requests automatically.

AQuA sidecar architecture (Source: Google Developer Blog Post )

Google evaluated 32 sessions from a multi-agent travel application, identifying 42 findings grouped into nine candidate clusters. The verifier rejected three unsupported clusters after checking up to three full transcripts per candidate cluster, leaving six verified issues. Two involved bypassing seat availability checks and losing a traveler's vegan preference during delegation.

After developers modified prompts and replayed the sessions, seat-selection bypasses fell from 15 sessions to two, dietary-preference omissions dropped from seven to zero, and sessions passing all checks increased from five to 13. These results came from controlled replay, not production traffic.

The Google blog post states,

> An insight is its citations, not a self-reported confidence score.

Findings link to supporting traces, and proposed root causes must reference valid lines in the deployed snapshot. AQuA tracks findings as NEW , RECURRING , or automatically RESOLVED after 14 days without being observed. Sampling can miss rare failures, and replay may not reproduce external state.

Reacting to the announcement on LinkedIn , Dmytro Aprelenko , engineering manager at Redcore, wrote ,

> Agent orchestration definitely needs better continuous diagnosis to catch these loops early.

AQuA validates source references and links findings to supporting traces. Cluster verification filters false positives, though it cannot confirm every session exhibits the same failure. Google's Agent Platform evaluation service supports regression testing and production quality monitoring, while Arize Phoenix provides open-source tracing and evaluation. AQuA focuses on grouping production failures and linking verified findings to deployed source code.

Google identifies sampling limits and incomplete reproduction of external state as constraints. Its open-source implementation helps teams integrate production agent diagnosis into development and evaluation workflows.

Google Cloud has made spend caps generally available on Cloud Billing Budgets, letting customers pause new usage of a service in a project once a monthly budget is reached, without deleting resources. The GA release adds an API, estimated live costs that trigger caps within minutes for AI services, and automatic monthly resets, but enforcement remains limited to Gemini API, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Cloud Run, and Cloud Run functions.

A spend cap is a budget with enforcement attached: according to the documentation , when estimated spend on the capped service reaches the target amount, new requests to that service in that project are blocked, in-flight requests run to completion and are charged, persistent resources keep running, and nothing is deleted. Usage covered by committed-use discounts is paused along with pay-as-you-go usage, while Provisioned Throughput for AI models is never halted. Billing administrators and project owners receive alerts at 50, 80, and 100 percent of the cap.

The company changed three things between the July public preview and the GA release:

- Caps can now be created, lifted, and deleted through the existing Cloud Billing Budgets API, which the company suggests wiring into project provisioning, so a new sandbox gets a cap on creation.

- Enforcement for AI services now runs on estimated live costs shown in Cost Reports rather than on settled billing data, which can lag by hours.

- A triggered cap resets automatically at the start of the next month; in preview, the block stayed in place until someone lifted it in the console, an option that remains.

(Source: Google blog post )

The limits are as specific as the features: a cap covers one project and one service for a calendar month, so folders, organizations, labels and multi-service budgets are out of scope, as are reseller accounts and subscription charges such as Gemini Enterprise seats. The estimate that drives enforcement is calculated at list price and excludes credits and discounts. Enforcement is also not instant: the documentation states that "any cost overages are billed as normal" and advises setting the cap "slightly below your absolute limit." Compute Engine, Cloud Storage, and networking are not among the eligible services, which means the cap addresses a runaway model or agent loop and not a forgotten GPU instance.

The narrower scope drew criticism when the preview expanded in October. On a Hacker News thread, one commenter who had asked Google for the capability a year earlier to control AI spend called the result "very crude, not granular like the rich IAM system," noting the four-product, month-only design. Another observed that Cloud Run had been added that morning, so the service list was still growing.

Developer Simon Willison argued in October that pay-by-usage services should default to hard caps, because coding and personal agents make it far easier to spin up code that calls paid APIs, and that "most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill." He cited Google's caps alongside a project-level spend limit in AWS's new account experience, which pauses the whole project and stops its resources when reached, preserving data for 90 days, and which AWS is rolling out to a limited number of customers. Azure's spending limit remains confined to free accounts and credit-based subscriptions; Microsoft states it isn't available for subscriptions with commitment plans or with pay-as-you-go pricing.

Spend caps pair with early anomalies, a daily baseline model that flags directional cost variances per service and names the top SKUs behind a spike, which Google positions as the detection half of the same control loop. Both are configured from the Budgets and Alerts page in the Billing console or through the Budgets API .

# Inkitt Builds a One-Shot PR Creator with Resumable Agent Orchestration

Nov 04, 2026 2 min read

by

- Leela Kumili

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

Inkitt has built a o ne-shot pull request (PR) creator that automates small, low-risk software changes, from task intake to a draft PR ready for testing and review. Triggered through Slack, Linear, or an API call from another agent, the workflow runs on remote infrastructure, reducing the need for developers to set up and supervise coding agents locally. Inkitt reported that the system was shipping code daily in a technical article published by Inkitt Tech.

The Agi Letkiewicz Tanner Lead Engineer at Inkitt, described it as

> Event-driven orchestrator that coordinates short-lived agent containers rather than relying on a fixed pipeline.

Individual stages handle specification, implementation, verification, CI failure repair, and merge conflict resolution. The orchestrator persists each run in a database, allowing execution to resume from its recorded state.

Inkitt’s one-shot PR creator architecture (Source: Inkitt Blog Post )

The orchestrator separates decision-making from side effects. Its core transition function maps the current run state and incoming event to the next action without directly accessing a database, network, or language model. The orchestrator retains credentials for external systems, while agent containers receive short-lived repository tokens and model credentials. They cannot directly access Slack or Linear credentials, cloud identities, or arbitrary network connections. A separate check inspects the actual Git diff to ensure changes do not touch restricted paths.

Inkitt limits automation to changes within predefined boundaries. The workflow rejects tasks involving database migrations, schema or shared contract changes, CI and container build configuration, authentication, payment code, or package additions and updates. Verification, CI repair, and merge conflict resolution each have a maximum of two attempts. Duplicate webhook deliveries are handled through deduplication and conditional database writes, applying the principle of idempotent operations to workflows that may retry or receive repeated events. For CI completion, the orchestrator queries GitHub to determine whether all relevant jobs have finished instead of treating every job event as completion of the entire workflow.

Tanner wrote, describing the implementation challenges around idempotency, locking, retry budgets, and permissions.

> The model was the easy part.

The design shares some safeguards with other coding agents but uses a different orchestration model. GitHub Copilot’s cloud agent also restricts agent permissions and requires human review before merging, while SWE-agent focuses on solving repository issues through a model-driven interface for browsing, editing, and executing code. Inkitt’s account emphasizes persistent workflow state, bounded retries, and centralized control of external actions.

Human approval remains part of Inkitt’s process. The system opens draft PRs, cannot bypass branch protection or merge its own changes, and notifies requesters when CI passes and the changes reach staging. A person must mark a PR ready for review and manage reviewer requests and approval. For larger tasks, Inkitt also maintains a local version that keeps a human involved in the development process.

# JioHotstar Benchmarks Knowledge Bases for AI Coding Agents

Nov 11, 2026 2 min read

by

- Leela Kumili

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

JioHotstar evaluated six approaches to helping AI coding agents navigate large codebases , finding that structural code search performed well on clearly defined engineering tasks, while semantic retrieval helped more with ambiguous requirements. The evaluation also found that adding retrieval layers did not consistently improve task completion or reduce token consumption.

Abhishek Bansal , Senior Staff Engineer at JioHotStar, compared filesystem tools, Sourcebot , Graphify , CocoIndex Code, Repowise , and an in-house retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline. The team evaluated the approaches using subsets of SWE-bench and CodeScaleBench , alongside a custom question-answering harness for JioHotstar's codebase. The experiments used Claude Sonnet as the solving model and measured task accuracy, token consumption, agent turns, and tool usability.

JioHotstar’s benchmark setup for evaluating code retrieval approaches for AI coding agents. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post )

The filesystem baseline, which relied on locally checked out repositories and standard search and file operations, remained competitive on concrete tasks. Sourcebot, which provides indexed text search, symbol definitions, references, and file reads, performed better than the baseline on harder SWE-bench Verified tasks while also costing less. On simpler SWE-bench Lite tasks, retrieval generally added overhead without consistently improving results.

CodeScaleBench showed a different pattern. Semantic retrieval helped more when agents had to interpret ambiguous problem descriptions and map them to implementation details that were not obvious from exact text or symbol searches. The findings suggest that retrieval approaches should be selected according to task characteristics rather than treated as interchangeable solutions.

The report also highlighted the importance of tool design. Agents frequently preferred familiar developer operations such as searching text, reading files, and locating symbols over higher-level abstractions that required additional verification.

Tool call breakdown by category across coding agent knowledge base approaches. (Source: JioHotstar Blog Post )

Siddharth Vaithinathan raised a broader architectural question in a LinkedIn post discussing the study :

> Whether coding agents should understand not only the code but also the company that produced it. He argued that repository indexing alone cannot capture why architectural decisions were made, which constraints shaped them, or what earlier incidents taught the engineering team.

Vaithinathan suggested extending agent knowledge beyond code and documentation to include architecture, constraints, decisions, rationale, incidents, and outcomes. Such context could help agents evaluate existing design choices before proposing changes, particularly in systems where historical operational experience influences architectural decisions.

Tarun Bhargava raises a relevant question for benchmark interpretation, particularly when evaluations use limited subsets and probabilistic models.

> Cost/accuracy numbers with multiple runs of the same setup.

JioHotstar's evaluation did not identify a single retrieval approach that performed best across all tasks. Instead, JioHotstar recommends retaining filesystem tools as a baseline, using structural search for concrete, code-focused problems and semantic indexing for ambiguous or cross-cutting requirements. JioHotStar engineering team also emphasizes measuring tool-use traces alongside task accuracy to determine whether retrieval reduces unnecessary exploration. The findings highlight the importance of matching retrieval capabilities to the programming task and how the agent navigates the codebase.

# Azure Logic Apps Standard Gets a Local CLI in Preview

Nov 12, 2026 3 min read

by

- Steef-Jan Wiggers

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

Microsoft has released a public preview of a local command-line interface for Azure Logic Apps Standard , shipped as the logicapp extension for the Azure CLI . It adds project creation, workflow authoring, a local runtime, connector and connection management, run inspection, and test scaffolding to a tool that until now only managed deployed apps, so that a Standard workflow can be created, run, and tested without Visual Studio Code.

The extension installs automatically the first time an az logicapp developer command runs on Azure CLI 2.67.0 or later , and adds 19 command groups with 64 commands beside the thirteen existing cloud-management commands, which it leaves untouched. On the authoring side, project create creates or adopts a local project; workflow create, set, export, and validate work on individual workflow.json files with offline validation by default, and runtime start, stop, and show manage a local host on port 7071, launching the Azurite storage emulator when the project is configured for development storage.

The remaining groups reach into running and deployed apps. connector and connection inspect built-in and managed connectors and wire connections into a project or a deployed app, run and trigger history start, wait on, cancel and resubmit executions and download an action’s recorded inputs and outputs, and deployment package produces what the documentation calls a deterministic deployment package. Named context shortcuts hold a target so later commands do not repeat it.

(Source: Microsoft Community Hub )

The doctor and test commands say the most about who the tool expects to be typing. runtime doctor only reads: project files, tool versions, cached bundle evidence, loopback ports. It "never installs, downloads, starts, stops, repairs, decrypts settings, changes context, or contacts cloud storage," and it exits 1 for a required failure and 2 when a required check comes back unknown. Testing is split into three steps for the same reason. test create scaffolds a native SDK test project and stops before restoring a package or running anything, test plan writes a preflight report without executing a test, and test run is the only command that builds and runs them, under a deadline. The announcement lists limitations on that last step. In the pull request that added the extension, author Riley Evans goes further: native SDK test code is trusted rather than sandboxed, and the agent bootstrap command does not exist yet.

Sagar Sharma, a Microsoft MVP, wrote on LinkedIn that this is deliberate. The CLI is "literally pitched as adding determinism to local AI-assisted coding": an agent validates, runs, inspects and tests, then repeats until the run is green, and secrets reach it through stdin rather than on the command line. Sharma had already called the CLI the sleeper hit of Microsoft's recent Logic Apps announcements in an earlier write-up , on the grounds that an agent without a deterministic way to validate and run a workflow is guessing. Named contexts, capability discovery and the handling of secrets were his evidence that someone had designed for that case.

Sonny Gillissen, also a Microsoft MVP, put the same point in terms of a team's week. A new hire clones a repository and has a local runtime up "in minutes, instead of hours." A coding assistant drafting a workflow from a business requirement works "with an authoritative shell instead of assumptions." Integration flows get tested from the CI/CD pipeline instead of by hand. He called the CLI a bridge from today's development process to a fully automated one and, in passing, said an agent could test a workflow locally "without ever touching Azure at all."

That passing remark is the one Christos Panagiotidis, a Microsoft MVP and certified trainer, would test first. His pilot plan is explicitly a proposal rather than a report of a run, and its two main cautions come straight from Microsoft's own walkthrough. That walkthrough uses live Azure and Microsoft 365 resources, and some of its commands change deployed connections, so a local run has remote effects, whatever the terminal suggests.

Microsoft itself notes that validation "does not establish authorization or business correctness." Panagiotidis adds a housekeeping point: CLI extensions do not update with the CLI, so anyone comparing results across runs needs the CLI, extension, runtime and project versions recorded next to each result.

Microsoft has said a broader command surface will follow soon. Until then, the designer stays in VS Code. The CLI edits workflow.json directly; it cannot change the state of a running local app, and the pull request's own limits section concedes that Linux CI results prove neither native SDK execution nor execution against live Azure.

# Pinterest Replaces Journey Clustering with 4B Qwen3 LLM, Reports Improved Engagement

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

by

- Matt Foster

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

Pinterest has moved its user-journey inference system from a multi-stage clustering pipeline to a fine-tuned 4-billion-parameter language model, reporting a 1.1% improvement in email click-through and 1.3% higher push opens.

Rather than clustering keywords into interests, the model examines users' activity histories to identify longer-term goals and feeds those journeys into Pinterest's existing recommendation infrastructure.

Pinterest defines a "journey" as a goal that connects interests, intent, and context across multiple sessions. Someone renovating a kitchen, for example, might search for cabinet designs, save countertop ideas, and later explore backsplash tiles or lighting. These interactions collectively suggest a coherent project rather than several unrelated interests.

("User Journey" - Source: Pinterest)

The company's previous system extracted keywords from user activity, grouped them using embeddings and hierarchical clustering, named the resulting clusters, and ranked them with additional models and diversity heuristics.

Although effective compared with earlier interest-based notifications, the approach could fragment related activities into separate journeys, produce generic labels, or mistake incidental engagement for sustained intent.

The new system instead treats journey inference as a generation task. A fine-tuned LLM reads a chronological history of up to 150 user actions across a 360-day window, alongside a compact user profile, and generates a ranked set of journey names. Search and save actions carry more weight than incidental clicks, while the prompt instructs the model to consider repeated engagement, recency, and specificity.

("Journey Inference" - Source: Pinterest)

The consolidation moved much of the previous system's ranking and filtering behavior into the prompt. Instructions discourage unrelated interests from being merged, suppress one-off activity and noisy automatically generated tags, and allow an empty result where there is insufficient evidence of a meaningful journey. Pinterest treats changes to these instructions as production launches rather than simple prompt edits.

To build the system without an extensive human-labelled dataset, Pinterest used frontier models to generate synthetic training examples from its user activity histories. These examples were used to fine-tune smaller open-weight Qwen3 models through supervised fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation (LoRA).

The team tested models ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, selecting the 4B model for its balance of inference quality and serving throughput.

Running the resulting model at Pinterest's scale presented a separate engineering challenge. The company deployed NVIDIA Dynamo in front of vLLM workers running on L40S GPUs, using continuous batching, PagedAttention, and prefix-cache-aware routing to improve inference efficiency.

(Journey Inference Architecture - Source: Pinterest)

However, one of the largest throughput improvements came from avoiding unnecessary inference altogether. The system tracks when each user's journeys were last generated and skips users processed within the preceding couple of days.

Pinterest evaluates journey quality through side-by-side comparisons, a separate LLM judge assessing relevance and support from user activity, and online experiments. Initial A/B testing in the US and Canada produced the reported 1.1% email click-through and 1.3% push-open improvements over the clustering-based system, alongside statistically significant engagement and retention gains.

The approach has parallels with Netflix's work on foundation models for personalised recommendations. Netflix has described learning from long sequences of member interactions to create representations that can be reused by downstream recommendation models.

While Netflix focuses on reusable preference representations and Pinterest generates explicit journey descriptions, both approaches use longer-term behavioural histories to enrich existing personalisation infrastructure rather than replace it entirely.
